tagline: From Owensboro’s bluegrass museum to the music-making places of Rosine
intro: The Bill Monroe Bluegrass Trail joins roads through Daviess, Hancock and Ohio counties, linking Owensboro with Lewisport, Hawesville and Rosine. Its river towns include Lewisport on the Ohio’s floodplain and Hawesville on the south bank and the hills above it. The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet lists the route as part of the Blues to Bluegrass Scenic Byway, with an original designated length of 113.782 miles.

The state designated the trail in January 2004 and added a US 231 segment in Ohio County in January 2007. Monroe’s own musical beginnings were near Rosine, where he was born on his family’s farm. He accompanied his uncle Pendleton Vandiver to fiddle dances, an experience that inspired “Uncle Pen”; fiddler and guitarist Arnold Shultz introduced him to the blues. The bluegrass genre took its name from Monroe’s band, the Blue Grass Boys.

From the McLean County line, follow the designated corridor through Saint Joseph and Sorgho to Owensboro, then toward Maceo, Lewisport and Hawesville. Turn inland along KY 69 toward Fordsville and Dundee, then follow the connecting roads to Rosine. The remaining drive passes through Beaver Dam and Hartford, then Centertown, ending on US 62 at the Muhlenberg County line.

moments.title: Owensboro
moments.text: The corner of First and Frederica streets near the Ohio River has a history beyond bluegrass. John G. Barnard founded the Modern Welding Company there in 1932; the Bluegrass Music Hall of Fame and Museum occupies that location now. Formerly called the International Bluegrass Music Museum, it is devoted to the music’s history and preservation and houses its Hall of Fame. Owensboro also hosts the bluegrass festival ROMP, short for River of Music Party. The city sits at a bend in the Ohio, and was first known as Yellow Banks.

moments.title: Lewisport
moments.text: Lewisport began as a ferry landing called Little Yellow Banks, with logging and flatboat building among its first main industries. James Prentis and his brother John laid out the town in 1837. The town occupies the Ohio River floodplain, and its history includes repeated floods and major fires. An early episode at the Pate House involved Abraham Lincoln as a defendant, charged with operating an unlicensed ferry across the Ohio. Squire Pate dismissed the case. The hearing took place in the east room of the log house, now a county landmark.

moments.title: Rosine
moments.text: Rosine’s general store and adjoining barn are both a historic place and a setting for bluegrass music. Musicians gather at the store and perform in the barn; a bronze disk on the barn memorializes Bill Monroe, who is buried in Rosine Cemetery. The store was built in 1933 and expanded in 1947. Edith and Everett Woosley enlarged it after buying it in 1943. Beside it stands a board-and-batten barn with vertical planks. The store and barn entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2003. Monroe’s musician brothers Birch and Charlie were also from Rosine.
moments.notice: The barn’s exterior uses vertical planks and board-and-batten construction.
